modules.title: First Contact
modules.why: The doorway moment — greet elders, introduce yourself, say it's a pleasure. Lock this first.

modules.title: Politeness & Repair
modules.why: Thanks, sorry, and the phrases that rescue you when you're lost.

modules.title: Toasts
modules.why: Russian tables run on toasts. A warm toast to the family lands huge.

modules.title: Family & In-Laws
modules.why: Kinship terms — you are the зять; her parents are your тесть & тёща.

modules.title: Food & Complimenting the Cook
modules.why: Praise the тёща's cooking; accept/decline more gracefully.

modules.title: Small Talk About You
modules.why: Who you are, where you're from, how you met your wife.

modules.title: Questions They'll Ask (Listening)
modules.why: Train your EAR for the questions relatives fire back at you.

modules.title: Core Verbs (reactivation)
modules.why: High-frequency verbs from Ekaterina's guide — я / вы forms.

items.hint: formal/ceremonial: [raz-re-shí-tye pred-stá-vi-tsa] — «Меня́ зову́т…» is the warmer everyday option
warmer than 'glad to be here' (a calque): [spa-sí-ba shto prí-nya-li] — при́няли stress on 1st syllable
items.note: Idiomatic guest gratitude — Russians thank the hosts for receiving them.

items.hint: your best rescue line: [ya ye-shchó u-chú rús-skiy]

items.en: How do you say … in Russian?
To getting to know each other!

items.note: NOT «На здоровье» — that is a reply to thanks, not a toast.

items.en: I want to make a toast to …

items.note: Referential term; address him by name+patronymic, not 'тесть'.

items.en: son-in-law (= what YOU are to them)

items.hint: [se-strá zhe-ný] — what people actually say; the formal kinship term is своя́ченица
the line that wins the table: [ya lyu-blyú vá-shu doch']
MALE form -лся; a woman says нае́лась
[pe-re-dáy-tye pa-zhá-lus-ta] — swap хлеб for any dish

items.en: I'm from the state of Missouri
items.hint: [ya is shtá-ta mis-sú-ri] — Миссу́ри is indeclinable; bare «Я из Миссу́ри» works too

items.en: Good, thank you (answer to 'how are you')
What do you do for work?
items.hint: lit. 'as whom do you work': [kyem vy ra-bó-ta-ye-tye]

error_types.label: Stress
error_types.repair: Replay native audio, mark the stressed vowel, then say it twice.

error_types.label: Vowel reduction
error_types.repair: Shadow the phrase slowly, then at table speed.

error_types.label: Gendered form
error_types.repair: Contrast the male/female form and produce the speaker-appropriate one.

error_types.label: Case / inflection
error_types.repair: Recall the whole verified phrase rather than assembling it word by word.

error_types.label: Register
error_types.repair: Choose the formal/polite option for elders and hosts.

error_types.label: Word order
error_types.repair: Repeat the complete model answer and compare chunks.

error_types.label: Listening misparse
error_types.repair: Listen with full text, then keyword hints, then no text.

error_types.label: Cultural usage
error_types.repair: Review the usage note and choose the phrase in context.

error_types.label: Forgot phrase
error_types.repair: Do cued recall, then production, then a role-play prompt.

contrast_sets.title: Toast vs. you're welcome
contrast_sets.usage_note: Use «За здоро́вье!» for a toast. Use «Пожа́луйста» for please / you're welcome.

contrast_sets.title: Formal elder address
contrast_sets.usage_note: Use formal «вы» forms and polite repair phrases with parents and elders.

contrast_sets.title: Joe's male speaker forms
contrast_sets.usage_note: Joe should keep male forms like «рад» and «наелся».

scenarios.goal: Greet the family formally and introduce yourself.
Accept, decline, and compliment food politely.
Raise a safe warm toast without using the wrong formula.
